newsitem.title: USA: French vote could help EMU drive - Camdessus.
newsitem.headline: French vote could help EMU drive - Camdessus.

text.p: IMF head Michel Camdessus said Thursday he thought European monetary union should go ahead on time in 1999, and said a snap election in France may strengthen the momentum toward a single currency.
"Elections are an essential element of democratic life. They are always a good thing," he said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
"Governments will come back with a new mandate from the people, they will have a wonderful opportunity to explain to people what is at stake.
"I think and I hope that if anything, these elections in the two countries (France and Britain) could strengthen the momentum toward EMU," he said.

French President Jacques Chirac earlier this week called an early two-round parliamentary election for May 25 and June 1 in what analysts see as seeking a mandate to push ahead with the tough austerity needed to qualify for monetary union.
The opposition Socialist party says it is not willing to impose a new bout of austerity to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Britain also holds a general election this month.
Camdessus said he thought EMU should be launched on time.
"I would suggest to go ahead and don't take the risk of the uncertainty ... any delay would create," he said.
He urged European countries to press ahead with budget cuts, and hinted these might have to get tougher.
"It would be a mistake now to stop this effort after accomplishing so much, and indeed to start acting more decisively," he said.

The International Monetary Fund said Wednesday that Germany, France and Italy all had to do more to bring their budget deficits to 3 percent of gross domestic product this year to qualify for a single currency.

And possibly more worryingly for Germany, which has insisted deficit reduction must be sustainable, it saw France's deficit-to-GDP ratio actually rising in 1998 without fresh action, to 3.4 percent from 3.3 percent.
Italy's ratio would jump to 4.1 percent from 3.3 percent, while the German deficit-to-GDP ratio would fall to 2.9 percent from 3.3 percent.
Camdessus acknowledged that the IMF's forecasts were slightly more pessimistic than those of the European Commission, but said both went in the same direction.
"I am more impressed by the convergence of views between the EU and the IMF than the divergence," he said.

"Even if we are a little bit more on the downside than they are, you know in this kind of thing, there is a broad margin of error. You are not in a kind of scientific, precise domain. I would not quarrel with half a point more or less."
The European Union will decide in late April/early May next year which countries qualify for a single currency, based on actual figures for this year.
